turns.user: Find these World Bank studies on technology in schools: WPS9288, WPS8665, WPS4836, and report 207830 on Uganda's EdTech readiness.
Which of these studies measured student learning outcomes, and which only reported device distribution or teacher training?

expected_sources.title: Technology in the Classroom and Learning in Secondary Schools

expected_sources.title: Re-Kindling Learning : eReaders in Lagos

text: The four records: (1) WPS9288, Technology in the Classroom and Learning in Secondary Schools (The Gambia, 2020-06-22); (2) WPS8665, Re-Kindling Learning: eReaders in Lagos (Nigeria, 2018-12-06); (3) WPS4836, The Use and Misuse of Computers in Education: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment in Colombia (2009-02); (4) Report 207830, Uganda - Examining Readiness to Use Technology in Schools: ETRI Results (2025-06-30), each with its abstract and link.

- WPS9288 (The Gambia): compares students in a computer-assisted math and science program with matched control students on a researcher-designed exam and the WASSCE school-leaving exam; math scores rose 0.54 SD on the researcher exam and 0.59 SD on the WASSCE, English by 3.87 percentage points (p. 5).

- WPS8665 (Lagos): randomized trial in junior secondary schools with baseline and endline tests of reading comprehension, math (TIMSS items) and non-verbal ability (p. 8); eReaders with curriculum textbooks gave imprecise gains of about 0.2 SD in reading, while non-curriculum content lowered scores (p. 12).

- WPS4836 (Colombia): randomized evaluation in 97 schools with 5,201 students using math and Spanish tests (p. 11); the program had little effect on test scores (p. 7). It also documents the inputs, refurbished computers plus about 20 months of in-school teacher training (p. 8), and finds teachers did not incorporate the computers into teaching.

- Report 207830 (Uganda ETRI): a readiness survey of 300 schools' principals and teachers plus student interviews (p. 27). It reports device availability (27% of working devices available to students, p. 14), connectivity (38% of schools online, p. 15) and teacher training and use (30% had initial training on ICT in teaching, 12% ICT professional development, p. 12; principal training, p. 11), but no test scores.

So three of the four measured learning; only the Uganda report is limited to devices, connectivity and teacher training. Strictly, none of the three evaluations reports only device distribution or teacher training.

right_sources: Finds all four records in turn 1 and reads (not just the abstracts of) the studies for the classification in turn 2.
grounded: Each classification cites the methods or results passage (page) that supports it; effect sizes, if given, match the papers.
scoped: Notes that the Colombia study also reports computers and teacher training while measuring learning, i.e. the categories are not exclusive.
